title: Title 18-A (former Maine Probate Code) — transition rule and material differences
scope: Per the project decision, the old code is covered as a transition note plus the handful of material substantive differences — NOT a full section-by-section derivation table.
disclaimer: Statutes for consideration only — not legal advice. Which code applies to a given estate is a legal determination; verify against current law and consult a Maine attorney.

transition.rule: Title 18-C took effect 2019-09-01. It applies to: (a) wills of, and intestate succession / elective share / exempt property / wrongful-death matters for, decedents who die on or after 2019-09-01; and (b) any probate proceeding pending on, or commenced on or after, the effective date, regardless of when the decedent died. Title 18-A (the former code) continues to govern the substantive succession rights for estates of decedents who died BEFORE 2019-09-01.
transition.savings: An act done before 2019-09-01 in any proceeding, and any accrued right, is not impaired by Title 18-C (§8-301).
transition.interest_of_justice: A court may apply the former procedure where the new Code's application would be infeasible or work an injustice (§8-301(2)).
transition.practical_test: The single most useful upstream question for almost every estate form: did the decedent die before or on/after 2019-09-01? Date of death selects the substantive code; the procedural code in a pending/new case is 18-C either way.

material_differences.current_18c: 18-C §2-202: elective share = 50% of the marital-property portion of the augmented estate. The marital-property portion (§2-203) is a percentage of the augmented estate that scales with marriage length — roughly 3% at <1 year, increasing to 100% at 15+ years.
material_differences.former_18a: Former 18-A: a flat one-third (1/3) of the augmented estate, not scaled by marriage length.
material_differences.why_it_matters: For the same surviving spouse and same assets, the elective-share amount can differ dramatically depending on whether the decedent died before or on/after 2019-09-01. Critical for DE-506 (Petition for Elective Share) and any intake that turns on a spouse's election.

material_differences.current_18c: 18-C §2-102: spouse takes the entire estate if no descendant or parent survives; first $300,000 plus 3/4 of the balance if a parent (but no descendant) survives; first $100,000 plus 1/2 of the balance where all of the decedent's surviving descendants are also the spouse's and the spouse has other descendants; and 1/2 of the estate where one or more surviving descendants are not the spouse's.
material_differences.former_18a: Former 18-A used lower base dollar amounts for the spouse's share. Treat any recalled 18-A figure as unverified — for a pre-2019 death, look up the 18-A figure that applied on the date of death.
material_differences.why_it_matters: Drives the heirship/share analysis behind DE-101 (intestate) and any heir-determination question.

material_differences.current_18c: 18-C Article 5 is the Maine Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship and Protective Proceedings Act (based on the 2017 uniform act): least-restrictive-alternative standard, supported decision-making, expanded categories of interested persons entitled to notice, and mandatory guardian/conservator plans and periodic reports.
material_differences.former_18a: Former 18-A Article 5 used a structurally different guardianship/conservatorship scheme with narrower notice and without the modern plan/report and least-restrictive framework.
material_differences.why_it_matters: All PP-*, GS-*, and N-1xx guardianship/conservatorship forms map to the new Article 5. Orders entered before 2019-09-01 may rest on different standards; registrations/transfers should be checked against the current act.

material_differences.current_18c: 18-C §3-1201: available when the entire estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $40,000 (adjusted for inflation), at least 30 days after death.
material_differences.former_18a: The former 18-A small-estate threshold was lower than $40,000. For a pre-2019 death, confirm the threshold and waiting period that applied then.
material_differences.why_it_matters: Eligibility for AF-102 (Small Estate Affidavit) and DE-603 (Closing Statement for Small Estate) turns on the threshold in effect.

material_differences.current_18c: 18-C added the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act (§§6-401 to 6-420), authorizing TOD deeds for real estate as a nonprobate transfer.
material_differences.former_18a: Former 18-A did not include a real-property transfer-on-death deed mechanism.
material_differences.why_it_matters: Affects what passes outside probate (and therefore what the inventory/estate actually contains) for deaths on or after 2019-09-01.

material_differences.current_18c: 18-C Article 10 is the Maine Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (§§10-101 to 10-118).
material_differences.former_18a: Maine first enacted RUFADAA in 2017 as Article 10 of the then-current code; it was carried into 18-C Article 10. Substance is continuous.
material_differences.why_it_matters: This is the statutory hook for a personal representative or conservator seeking access to a decedent's online accounts — see docs/digital-assets-access.md.
